item.title: AsyncAPI Miasma npm compromise, First VPN sanctions, and Grok Build data exposure
item.content:encoded:
Coordinated AsyncAPI Supply Chain Attack: Miasma RAT Delivered via Compromised CI/CD Pipelines in Two Repositories — Must Read

Attackers compromised push access to two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories and used legitimate GitHub Actions release workflows with npm OIDC provenance to publish malicious package versions containing a Miasma RAT dropper. The key lesson is that valid provenance proves a trusted pipeline built the package, but it does not prove the triggering commit was legitimate.

  • A coordinated supply chain attack on July 14, 2026 compromised two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories and produced malicious npm package versions for @asyncapi/generator, @asyncapi/generator-helpers, @asyncapi/generator-components, and @asyncapi/specs.
  • The attacker gained push access to the repositories and used the projects’ legitimate GitHub Actions release pipelines with npm GitHub OIDC trusted-publisher integration, so no npm token was stolen.
  • The malicious packages carried an obfuscated dropper that executed when the library was loaded during normal use, not during npm installation.
  • Static analysis showed the dropper fetched an IPFS-hosted second-stage sync.js payload and installed it in hidden OS-specific NodeJS directories before launching it detached and hidden.
  • The decrypted second-stage payload was identified as Miasma v3 and included multiple command-and-control channels, credential harvesting, persistence, lateral movement, shell execution, and self-destruct capabilities.

Microsoft Maps Three Salesforce Attack Paths Tied to a Year of ShinyHunters Activity — Must Read

Microsoft says ShinyHunters-linked actors spent a year stealing data from Salesforce environments by abusing trusted access rather than Salesforce flaws, including malicious OAuth consent, stolen vendor OAuth tokens, and misconfigured guest access. The key defense is to monitor and govern connected apps, OAuth scopes, API activity, and guest permissions, not just user logins.

  • Microsoft reported that attackers whose methods align with ShinyHunters accessed corporate Salesforce environments from mid-2025 into mid-2026 without exploiting a Salesforce platform flaw.
  • Microsoft mapped the activity to three intrusion paths: vishing that tricked employees into approving a malicious connected app, stolen OAuth tokens from compromised software vendors, and misconfigured guest access to Salesforce sites.
  • The vishing campaign involved attackers posing as IT support and persuading employees to authorize an attacker-controlled connected app disguised as Salesforce’s Data Loader tool.
  • In vendor-related incidents involving Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, and Klue, attackers used trusted integrations or stolen tokens to access Salesforce customer environments and export data.
  • Microsoft and Salesforce added Defender for Cloud Apps capabilities to surface Salesforce Real-Time Event Monitoring data, connected-app attribution, OAuth scopes, API context, and governance features for risky or unused connected apps.

Grok Build Uploads Entire Git Repositories to xAI Storage, Not Just Files It Reads — Should Read

xAI’s Grok Build CLI was found uploading entire tracked Git repositories, including commit history and some secrets, to xAI-controlled Google Cloud storage even when the model only needed specific files and model-improvement was turned off. xAI appears to have disabled the uploads server-side, but users who ran the tool should rotate any credentials that may have been read, tracked, or present in Git history.

  • A researcher testing xAI’s Grok Build CLI version 0.2.93 found it uploaded entire tracked Git repositories, including full commit history, to an xAI-controlled Google Cloud Storage bucket rather than only files needed for a coding task.
  • In one test on a 12 GB repository, traffic to the model endpoint was about 192 KB while the storage channel sent 5.10 GiB in 73 chunks of about 75 MB each.
  • The researcher cloned a captured Git bundle from the upload and recovered a file the agent had been explicitly told not to open, along with the repository’s full commit history.
  • Turning off the “Improve the model” setting did not stop the repository upload, and the server continued to return trace_upload_enabled: true during testing.
  • On July 13, the same 0.2.93 client stopped making storage requests after server-side settings changed to disable_codebase_upload: true and trace_upload_enabled: false, but xAI had not confirmed whether the change applied to every account or was permanent.

148 npm Packages Disguised as Student Proxies Turned Browsers Into a DDoS Botnet — Should Read

JFrog found 148 npm packages masquerading as student proxy sites that secretly turned visitors’ browsers into a DDoS botnet using HTTP and WebSocket floods. The campaign abused npm as free hosting rather than targeting developers at install time, and its remote loader means the operators could re-enable the attack without publishing new packages.

  • JFrog reported that 148 npm packages disguised as student web proxies turned visitors’ browsers into a distributed denial-of-service botnet for roughly two weeks in May.
  • The packages did not run malicious code at install time; instead, they hosted a proxy web app that loaded hidden browser-side modules when users visited the pages.
  • One hidden module fetched remote JavaScript from a mutable GitHub branch through jsDelivr, allowing the operators to change code running in visitors’ browsers without updating the npm packages.
  • An archived payload from May 30 sent repeated no-cors POST requests with large data bodies to cdn.caan.edu, which JFrog identified as the public domain of a nursing school in Matteson, Illinois.
  • A second module opened multiple WebSocket connections to a Wisp endpoint on lunaron[.]top and repeatedly sent valid Wisp CONNECT and CLOSE frames, which JFrog described as a control-plane attack against Wisp proxy servers.

US sanctions VPN, malware providers for enabling ransomware attacks — Should Read

The U.S. Treasury sanctioned First VPN Service, its administrator, and a Belarusian cryptor seller for providing infrastructure and tools that helped ransomware groups hide identities, evade detection, and attack U.S. organizations. The action follows an international law enforcement takedown of 1VPNS infrastructure tied to cybercrime worldwide.

  • The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned First VPN Service, its administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi, and Belarusian national Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev for enabling ransomware attacks against U.S. organizations.
  • First VPN Service advertised on cybercriminal forums that it kept no logs of user activity or identities and would not cooperate with law enforcement.
  • European law enforcement took down First VPN Service’s website and infrastructure in May with support from the FBI’s Boston Field Office as part of Operation Saffron.
  • Authorities seized 33 servers linked to First VPN Service across 27 countries, arrested its administrator, and exposed thousands of users associated with ransomware, fraud, and other malicious activity.
  • Ransomware operations using First VPN Service and Silayev cryptors have caused billions of dollars in losses to businesses and critical infrastructure providers across the United States.

Introducing the Silent Push Partner Program — Optional

Silent Push launched its Partner Portal and formal Channel Partner Program to support its 55+ global partners with sales, marketing, and co-sell resources for its preemptive threat intelligence offering. The program aims to accelerate partner-led adoption across EMEA, APJ, and other regions.

  • Silent Push is launching the Silent Push Partner Portal and officially announcing its Channel Partner Program.
  • Silent Push says it already has more than 55 global partners, including distributors, MSSPs, systems integrators, and technology resellers.
  • The Partner Portal provides branded assets, product collateral, white papers, datasheets, campaign assets, co-sell resources, and a direct line to the Silent Push team.
  • Silent Push says its proprietary Indicators of Future Attack data gives security teams visibility into adversary infrastructure before it is weaponized.
  • Silent Push plans to roll out partner spotlights, onboard new regional partners, and add training and enablement content to the portal over the coming weeks.
